chapter: Kansas City bands and the Blue Devils
title: Walter Page's bass tone and Gene Ramey
summary: Page's strength and big hands made the stage sway; Durham compares the big-toned bassists of the time and praises Gene Ramey.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Bass players: lineage, tone and technique

blocks.x: Tell me something about Walter Page. What do you remember of him in those days? I mean, he was a good musician, wasn't he?

One thing about Page, he could master tone or filler. He could be heard without amplifying. Big hands and arms, I don't know how he hit those notes, but when he would hit a note, the vibration would vibrate in any room, and the stage would sway.
Then he was a strong guy, wasn't he?
Yeah, big, strong guy. Then he would
hug the bass like this, and he said his body and things had a lot to do with the tone of the bass, too.

And the way he'd hit the note, you know. Like, a lot of guys pick it like this? He used to hit those notes. Big, like that. That was the style then, and Mose Allen wasn't a great bass player, but he used that style and -- he didn't play many notes, though.
Well, he sort of -- he slapped more.

Yeah, he didn't have much tone, but Stanfield and Hawkins kind of had a big tone like that. But at the present time, Gene Ramey is the guy with that big solid tone. Not naming other musicians, but he's a little bigger than some of the greater guys in those days.
They toned him down. Because I think using that amplifier -- leaning on the amplifier a lot, some of the guys.
But it always seemed to me, too, that Gene Ramey sort of somehow held the notes a little longer than most of them.
A sort of longer sound on them.
